opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really telling example, and it's one I find myself coming back to quite a lot. Reddit had a very strong team. They had spent years building up domain expertise about their users, their communities, how people engage with content, and they'd encoded all of that into hand-crafted features: aggregations, counts, time windows, joins across lots of tables. That's the classic way of doing machine learning on enterprise data. You take your relational database, you have data scientists and engineers flatten it into one big feature table, and then you train something like a gradient-boosted tree on top.

The interesting thing is what happens when you stop doing that flattening by hand. The approach we've been pushing is to treat the database itself as a graph. Every row is a node, and the foreign-key relationships are edges. Then you let a graph neural network, or more recently a relational foundation model, learn directly over that structure. The model figures out which signals matter, how far to look across the relationships, and how to aggregate over time, instead of a human deciding that ahead of time.

So my interpretation of the Reddit result is not that domain expertise doesn't matter. Those people knew their business extremely well. The point is that a human can only explore a tiny slice of the possible feature space. You think of a few hundred, maybe a few thousand features, and you're limited by time, by intuition, and by the cost of maintaining all of those pipelines. The model can explore a vastly larger space of multi-hop, temporal patterns that nobody would think to write down. When you give it the raw relational structure, it finds signal that was simply left on the table.

It's the same story we saw in computer vision and NLP. People spent decades engineering features like SIFT and HOG, or linguistic features, and then deep learning came along and learned representations end to end that beat all of that. I think structured enterprise data is going through that transition right now. It's been the last holdout because the data doesn't look like images or text, it looks like a bunch of interlinked tables. Once you realize those tables are really a graph, you can bring representation learning to it.

The practical upshot is also important. Beyond the accuracy gains, you dramatically cut the time to build a model. Instead of months of feature engineering for each new prediction task, you can define the task, point the model at the database, and get a strong model very quickly. That changes what an organization can afford to predict. And the domain experts can spend their time on the questions that actually need human judgment: what should we be predicting, how do we act on it, is it fair, is it aligned with the business, rather than on writing the hundred-and-first aggregation query.

r001.rationale: The response describes Reddit’s years of expertise and hand-crafted features, but says the model found signal left on the table and could explore a much larger feature space. It does not suggest Reddit had already captured most of the improvement available from that work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually a really interesting story, and I think it says something broader about where machine learning on graphs is heading. So at Reddit, the advertising team had spent years, really, building up domain expertise. They had a very careful set of hand-engineered features: who the user is, what communities they participate in, what they've clicked on, what the advertiser is, and so on. And this was good work. It wasn't that the manual features were bad. These are smart people who understand the product deeply.

But the thing is, Reddit is fundamentally a graph. You have users, you have subreddits, you have posts, you have comments, you have ads, and all of these are connected. And when you build features by hand, you are essentially trying to summarize that graph structure into a fixed set of numbers. You can only encode the relationships you thought to look for. So you might say, "this user is subscribed to these ten communities," but you're not capturing that those communities are themselves related to other communities that are related to the advertiser's audience, three or four hops away.

What we found when we applied graph neural networks, this was work that grew out of the PinSage line of research, is that the model learns to aggregate information across those hops automatically. It's learning the features rather than having a human specify them. And the improvement we saw on top of the existing system was substantial, which honestly surprised some of the folks internally, because they thought the manual features had captured most of what mattered.

So how do I interpret it? I think two things. One, it tells you that there is signal in the structure of the data that is very hard for humans to articulate as features. It's not that the domain experts were wrong, it's that the relational information is combinatorially rich, and no one can enumerate it by hand. And two, it suggests that domain expertise and learned representations are complementary rather than competing. The best results came from using the embeddings alongside the existing features, not replacing them. The expertise tells you what the problem is and how to evaluate it. The model tells you what patterns in the graph actually predict the outcome. I think that combination is going to be the standard pattern, not just in advertising, but anywhere the data is relational.

r001.rationale: The response says Reddit had spent years building careful manual features and that some people thought they captured most of what mattered. It does not clearly say those features had already delivered much of the improvement available; the claim is presented as an internal belief that the graph model then challenged.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is that domain expertise and machine learning are complementary. You can spend a lot of time understanding the problem and designing features, and those features can be very useful. But you're still making choices about which patterns you think matter and which interactions to capture.

Machine learning can take that further by learning combinations of signals that would be difficult to specify manually. In a setting like Reddit, the context of a community and the interests of a user can interact in complicated ways. A signal might be useful in one context and much less useful in another.

So I would interpret the improvement as evidence that there was still structure in the data that the manually designed system wasn't capturing. It doesn't mean the domain expertise was wasted. That expertise helps you decide what information to give the model, what objective to optimize, and how to evaluate whether the improvement is meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says manually designed features remained useful but failed to capture some structure. It does not suggest Reddit had already extracted much of the improvement available from domain expertise and engineered features.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it shows how difficult it is to capture all the relevant signals by hand. You can spend a lot of time understanding the domain and engineering features, and that work is valuable. But you’re still making assumptions about which patterns matter and how they interact. Machine learning can discover combinations that you wouldn’t necessarily think to encode explicitly.

For advertising, the problem is really about matching: understanding the context, understanding a person’s interests, and identifying which ad might be relevant. Those relationships can be quite complex. So I wouldn’t interpret the improvement as domain expertise being unnecessary. I’d interpret it as domain expertise helping us formulate the problem, while learning from data gives us a more powerful way to capture the patterns within it.

r001.rationale: The response says domain expertise and manual features are valuable but limited, and that machine learning can find additional patterns. It does not say Reddit had already extracted much of the improvement available from that work.
